summary: The root مَيْل (myl) describes an inclining or bending motion, often in one's gait, swaying from side to side. It can also mean to deviate or turn away from a path or course.
lane: 6 تَمَايَلَ فِى مِشْيَتِهِ ذ [ He affected an inclining of his body, or a bending, or he inclined his body, or bent, from side to side, in his gait; a meaning well known, and still common]; (S;) syn. تَثَنَّى . (Har, p. 269.) -b2- See تَزَايُغٌ . -b3- تَمَايَلَتْ فِى مِشْيَتِهَا and signify the same. (TA.) -b4- تَمَايَلَ إِلَى الشَّىْءِ ; and عَنْ طَرِيقِهِ : i. q. تَجَانَفَ [ He affected a deviation, or purposely deviated from his course, &c.] (TA in art. جنف .)

headwords.def: [ He, or it, inclined, leant, bent, propended, tended, declined, deviated, or deflected. ] مَالَ مَعَهُ and He conformed with, and assisted, or aided, him. (TA.) مَالَ إِلَيْهِ He loved him. (TA.) He wronged him. (TA.) He was, or became, inimical to him. مَالَتِ الدَّابَّةُ مِنْ رِجْلِهَا (K, art. غمز,) i. q. ظَلَعَتْ [It limped ]. (TA.)
مَيَّلَ بَيْنَ شَيْئَيْنِ He wavered, or vacillated, between two things. (S, MA.) See 10.
He inclined towards him reciprocally: and مَايَلَا they two inclined each towards the other. (TK, art. هود.) See also مَالَ مَعَهُ in 1.
تَمَيَّلَ See 6. تَمَيَّلَ بِالقَوْلِ He vacillated in the saying: see تَرَجَّحَ.

تَمَايَلَ فِى مِشْيَتِهِ [ He affected an inclining of his body, or a bending, or he inclined his body, or bent, from side to side, in his gait; a meaning well known, and still common]; (S;) syn. تَثَنَّى. (Har, p. 269.) See تَزَايُغٌ. تَمَايَلَتْ فِى مِشْيَتِهَا and signify the same. (TA.) تَمَايَلَ إِلَى الشَّىْءِ; and عَنْ طَرِيقِهِ: i. q. تَجَانَفَ [ He affected a deviation, or purposely deviated from his course, &c.] (TA in art. جنف.)
and استمال بِقَلْبِهِ, (S, K,) He inclined him, and his heart. (K.) اِسْتَمَالَهُ He attracted him to himself; or sought to make him incline. (MA.) استمال is a quasi-pass. of. (K, * TA.)

as used by the Arabs, [ A mile: ] The distance to which the eye reaches along land: accord. to the ancient astronomers, three thousand cubits: accord to the moderns, four thousand cubits: but the difference is merely verbal; for they agree that its extent is ninety-six thousand digits; [about 5166 English feet;] each digit being the measure of six barley-corns, each placed with its belly next to another; but the ancients say that the cubit is thirty-two digits; which makes the mile…
(?) of a مَحَالَة of a well: see ثِنَايَةٌ.
[ i. q. مُتَمَايِلٌ, Inclining much ]. (A, art. فيد.) See سَيَّالٌ.
Swaying on horseback: see an ex. of its pl. مِيلٌ in a verse cited voce أَشْعَلَ. عِمَّةٌ مَيْلَآءُ: see قَفْدَآءُ.

امالةُ الأَلِفِ The inclining of the sound of ا when quiescent, after fet-hah, towards the sound of ى; so that the fet-hah, with that ا, composes a sound the same as that of the long “ e ” in the English word “ there. ” This is accordant with present usage; and I have not found any learned Arab who asserts otherwise. See also نَابٌ, and حَجَّاجٌ, and مَشُوبٌ.

headword_note: Lane organises by verb form and principal noun, not by every inflected form. A word with no headword entry falls back to the root meaning; nothing is inferred.
mentions_note: Forms Lane discusses inside another entry rather than defining as a headword. Values index into headwords[].
